articles.title: What will Twins’ rotation look like come 2027?
articles.summary: This is the first in a series of five stories examining some of the biggest questions facing the Twins this offseason. The Twins enter this offseason with an...
articles.body:
This is the first in a series of five stories examining some of the biggest questions facing the Twins this offseason.

The Twins enter this offseason with an enviable amount of starting pitching depth, boasting eight starters who have major league experience under team control for 2027 and a rotation that could be headed by a pair of all-stars.

Of course, the Twins also felt strongly about their rotation depth a year ago, too, only to see it quickly erode. Pablo López and David Festa never threw a pitch last season, Mick Abel didn't pitch after April, and underperformance led to them to move on from Simeon Woods Richardson in May.

With López, Joe Ryan, Taj Bradley, Bailey Ober, Dean Kremer, Connor Prielipp, Zebby Matthews and Abel all under team control for 2027, the Twins have a number of decisions to make this winter.

Will they trade from this group? And by the time they break camp, which five starters will crack the rotation?

The first four in that group will all be free agents at season's end, which seems to make it more likely the Twins trade some of that depth to bolster other areas of the roster.

"It's definitely something we'll want to assess," general manager Jeremy Zoll said. "And, in a perfect world, if you can take areas of strength and exchange those for areas of weakness and build a better club in aggregate, that's what we're trying to do, and that'll be on our minds."

Ryan, an all-star in July, could be a candidate, though with one year left on his deal — and coming off a tough second half derailed in part by a glute injury — his trade value isn't what it once was.

Ober, due a raise to around $6.9 million in arbitration, per MLB Trade Rumors estimates, could be another trade candidate. Though he bounced back somewhat from his career-worst 2025 season, his diminished velocity and strikeout rate could lead to him being an odd-man out in the rotation in 2027.

He could also potentially be a non-tender candidate.

Complicating a potential trade is the near-certain lockout, which would go into effect when the Collective Bargaining Agreement expires in early December and could influence how teams approach the offseason trade market early.

"It's a lot less clear how the trade market will operate in November," Zoll said. "In normal offseasons, you kind of can bounce back and forth between free-agent discussions and trade discussions, but I don't know how active markets will be in November on the trade front — for guys that that are expiring after 2027 or not."

There also are natural questions concerning López and Abel, both of whom are returning from season-ending elbow surgeries. López had his ulnar collateral ligament repaired in February, and Abel had an arthroscopic surgery in July.

Bradley, named the Twins' pitcher of the year after posting a 3.73 ERA across 31 starts and recording 205 strikeouts, will have a spot in the rotation, as should Kremer, acquired in a midseason trade. Prielipp established himself this season and looks as if he could be a potential long-term piece.

Abel showed flashes of his promise after beating out Matthews for a rotation spot at the beginning of this season. Matthews did as well, though he also struggled with consistency.

The Twins will have plenty of time to sift through their options between now and spring training but at a baseline, like where they're starting from.

"Starting pitching depth … feels really, really encouraging as a starting point," Zoll said. "That might create (trade) opportunities for us. It might. But we also know you can never have too much starting pitching."

articles.title: Brewers fans' $1,000 'Timeless Ticket' purchase in 2015 paying off with World Series seats
articles.summary: The decade-old promotion promised fans a ticket to any future home game, including the World Series.
articles.body:
A $1,000 purchase back in 2015 may be paying off for some Milwaukee Brewers fans over a decade later.

As the Brewers prepare to play in the World Series for the first time since 1982 , there could be some in attendance at American Family Field who took advantage of a unique promotion following a season where the the team finished out of the playoff hunt for the third straight year.

Any fan who plunked down $1,000 for a " Timeless Ticket " — a 1-pound brass ticket featuring the engraved named of the owner — sold by the team were able to redeem it for one ticket to any future home game, which included Opening Day and playoff games. World Series games were also part of the deal.

The promotion had no expiration date, as the team wrote 11 years ago the redemption could happen "this season or 2050." The offer also allowed "Timeless Ticket" holders the ability to purchase three additional tickets at face value.

Some of the 1,000 fans who took advantage of the limited edition promotion have cashed in since the initial announcement. Now that the Brewers are back in the Fall Classic, there are some who held on to their "Timeless Ticket" and are eager to get a seat.

Fans had to submit a form in order to secure their World Series seat and will learn next week which game they will attend and where their seat will be located. "Ticket redemption is subject to availability at time of redemption," the Brewers website says .

The Brewers told 12 News that they "have been working diligently on all inquiries in the order they are received."

The 2026 World Series will see the Brewers play either the Cleveland Guardians or Tampa Bay Rays. Game 1 will take place on Friday, Oct. 23 in Milwaukee.

articles.title: Royals’ $3Bn Downtown Ballpark Wins With Stunning New Renderings
articles.summary: New images of the Royals' $3bn ballpark show a beautiful design, but fans demand competitive spending before the 2030 move to downtown.
articles.body:
The Kansas City Royals have finally shown the world what their $3 billion downtown dream looks like, and the reaction is mixed with a sharp edge. Architects released six new images on Thursday that paint a bright picture for the city, yet the real test remains whether ownership will spend enough to win. This is a huge win for the look, but the team must prove it will build a contender, not just a pretty place to sit.

The new venue is set to cost about $1.9 billion, with the rest of the funds going toward an 85-acre mixed-use development around it. The Kansas City Council approved plans for a $600 million commitment to support the project, while private investors and the Royals ownership cover the rest. Populous, a local Kansas City firm, designed the stadium that will seat 34,000 fans. Per talkSPORT , the design team was an easy choice for the front office because they wanted the best fan experience in Major League Baseball.

Fans are reacting to the new look with a mix of excitement and caution. One fan told talkSPORT, "I wasn't a fan of moving, but the stadium looks so beautiful. Hope it all comes together like this." Another added, "This looks absolutely stunning, I just hope management and ownership are going to spend to make them competitive." The renders show a modern structure that honors the city, but the hope for a winning team hangs in the air.

Royals CEO John Sherman defended the local choice for the architects, noting the firm's global reputation. "We could have searched the world over for the leading sports architecture firm in the world, but it's right here in Kansas City," Sherman said via MLB.com. Construction is set to begin in May 2027, giving the city three years to prepare for the big shift.

A third fan told talkSPORT, "I am really excited for the move, they have all looked beautiful, I just hope that they can follow through on what's been promised." This sentiment hits the core of the issue for Royals fans who have waited decades for a return to downtown. The building is only half the battle; the team on the field must be ready to play when the gates open.

The project represents a massive change for a franchise that has called the Truman Sports Complex home since 1973. A fourth commenter on the new images said, "Its beautiful, a huge win for downtown Kansas City." A fifth fan concluded, "I love a lot of the details. I can't wait to enjoy this new stadium! I see so many pieces of History that aren't being forgotten." These words show deep pride in the design and the history of the team.

Yet the clock is ticking toward the 2030 move, and the pressure is on the owners to back up the beautiful blueprints with a winning roster.

Ruth Werning, a 104-year-old Milwaukee Brewers fan, has the perfect gift in mind for her birthday next month.

Speaking to Denise Craig of WISN 12 in Milwaukee, Werning would love to see her beloved Brewers give her a World Series title.

"Oh my, would it ever," Werning said when asked whether a championship would be a big gift. "I'm able to get around. Put me on a bus, put me on an airplane. Oh, I think I'd have something to look forward to."

The Brewers clinched a berth in the World Series by sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS.

Werning will celebrate her 105th birthday in November, so it would be a little bit of an early present since Game 7 of the Fall Classic is scheduled to be played on Oct. 31.

Brewers fans might know Werning from her 2024 appearance at American Family Field when she threw out the ceremonial first pitch during a regular-season game against the Dodgers.

Milwaukee won that game 6-4, so the club might want to see if Werning can attend a World Series game as a good-luck charm.

Born in 1921, Werning is 48 years older than the Brewers franchise. They played their first MLB season in 1969 and this will be just their second World Series appearance after losing to the St. Louis Cardinals in seven games in 1982.

articles.title: Rays even ALCS at two games apiece with Game 4 win over Guardians after series postponement
articles.summary: The Tampa Bay Rays evened the ALCS at two games apiece as Yandy Diaz's two-out, two-run homer in the ninth sealed a dominant 7-3 Game 4 win.
articles.body: It will take at least six games to crown an American League champion. The Tampa Bay Rays tied the ALCS at two games apiece, winning Game 4 over the Cleveland Guardians 7-3. The Guardians got on the board early, as Chase DeLauter drove in Steven Kwan with an RBI single in the first. But Cleveland's offense was quiet after that. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Tampa Bay got the run back with a two-out rally in the third — Yandy Diaz doubled, and then Jonathan Aranda drove him in to tie the game. In the sixth inning, Junior Caminero smoked an RBI double with runners on first and second and none out to give the Rays a 2-1 lead, but they squandered an opportunity to tack on more. The Rays began the next frame with runners on second and third, no outs and the top of their order at the plate. Diaz struck out, but Aranda brought both of the runs in to give Tampa Bay a 4-1 lead. He would score on a sac fly two batters later. In the top of the ninth, Diaz added some huge insurance runs with a two-out, two-run jack that DeLauter just missed robbing. Any lead is comfortable for All-Star closer Bryan Baker, but four runs was a walk in the park. He got a double play after a leadoff single, and he struck out Angel Martinez to end the game. articles.title: Even with the home run that wasn't, Junior Caminero and the Rays' offense finally break through in ALCS Game 4
articles.summary: In Tampa Bay's victory to tie the series, Caminero finally found the big swing he'd been looking for.
articles.body:
CLEVELAND — Junior Caminero would not be denied.

The Tampa Bay Rays' superstar slugger was still seeking his first signature postseason moment going into ALCS Game 4 on Saturday at Progressive Field . And with Tampa Bay down 2-1 to the Cleveland Guardians in the series, it was crucial for the Rays' best player to make his presence felt sooner rather than later.

Caminero was also coming off an uncharacteristically sloppy showing at the plate in Game 3. The 23-year-old wasn't the only Rays hitter who didn't muster much in Tampa Bay's 3-2 loss , but Caminero's struggles stood out. No one in the majors swings the bat faster than Caminero, but he's still able to make contact and avoid punching out at an above-average clip. That, in a nutshell, is what makes him special. But on Thursday against a trio of terrific right-handers in Gavin Williams, Daniel Espino and Cade Smith, Caminero struck out four times for just the second time in his career and first since Aug. 17, 2025 . This after he drove in only one run across his first five games of the postseason.

"I would say Cami is highly motivated to get going, and rightfully so. Because every challenge that he's met or big game that he's been in, he's found his way to have some success and really impact the game," Rays manager Kevin Cash said ahead of Game 4.

"[Game 3] was not his best game. Gotta credit the Guardians' pitching for the way they attacked him. But he's going to make the adjustments needed and find a way to get his name in the paper in the best possible way moving forward."

Those adjustments were on full display Saturday, as Caminero finally found the big swing he'd been looking for in Tampa Bay's 7-3 victory to even the ALCS at two games apiece. After Espino walked Jonathan Aranda and Chandler Simpson to lead off the sixth inning, Caminero strolled to the plate in a tie game with a golden opportunity to push the Rays ahead. This was Caminero's third encounter with Espino in the series, and the first two had not gone well. In Game 1, Caminero swung through three fastballs at 98.2, 99.4 and 98.6 mph. In Game 3, Espino cranked up the heat further and got the same result by pumping 100.6, 100.6 and 100.3 mph past Caminero, all at the top of the zone.

In Game 4, Espino once again came with the high heat, but this time, it was only 97.9 mph — and Caminero didn't miss it. Third time was the charm: Caminero blistered the ball over a leaping José Ramírez and down the left-field line to drive in Aranda and make it 2-1 Tampa Bay.

It wasn't just the redemption against Espino that made Caminero's sixth-inning double so satisfying. It was also how his first two at-bats of the game had unfolded. Caminero's eagerness to break through was evident in his first trip to the plate. Moved down to fourth in the batting order after hitting third in the Rays' first six games this October, Caminero came up to bat after Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana made an error to allow Chandler Simpson to reach. But Caminero jumped at a first-pitch cutter from Cleveland opener Shawn Armstrong and grounded out weakly to second base. Statcast measured his swing at an elite 81.6 mph, but the ball left his bat at a harmless 73.7 mph to end the inning.

When Caminero led off the fourth, RBI singles from Chase DeLauter and Aranda had the game knotted at 1. In his second at-bat, this time facing Cleveland left-hander Foster Griffin, Caminero's unrivaled right-handed cut made a more familiar kind of contact — the kind the Rays had been waiting for all October.

After landing a sweeper for a called strike one, Griffin attacked with a 92-mph fastball above the zone, and Caminero pounced. This time, his swing speed checked in at only 79.7 mph — still elite — but the barrel met the ball flush, sending it sizzling toward straightaway center field at 110.7 mph with a 29-degree launch angle. Similar combinations of batted ball metrics have quite literally produced only home runs since Statcast began tracking in 2015.

But on this especially chilly night in Cleveland — 46 degrees was the lowest recorded first-pitch temperature for a postseason game since Game 1 of the 2019 NLCS in St. Louis — it was not to be.

Guardians center fielder Petey Halpin bolted back toward the fence and began backpedaling once he reached the warning track. It briefly looked like he lost track of the ball, but at the last moment, Halpin recovered and made a falling catch just in front of the deepest part of the outfield wall.

As the sellout Progressive Field crowd of 33,355 went wild, the Rays and Caminero were positively stunned. Rays reliever Tyler Wells was in the bullpen deep beyond the right-center-field fence, so his view of Caminero's batted ball's landing spot was somewhat obscured. But when Caminero connected, its destination appeared certain.

"Whenever I saw everyone cheering, I was really confused," Wells said afterward. "I was like, 'What happened? Did this guy scale up half the wall? Did he pull a Spider-Man?' But it didn't even make it to the wall."

"I've seen that a lot of times this year," Simpson said later. "And most likely, it is going over the fence."

Did Caminero think it was gone? "100 percent."

But it was not. At a projected 410 feet, it was tied for the farthest batted ball hit for an out at Progressive Field in the Statcast Era.

"Found a glove that time," Simpson said. "But he was able to come up big for us later in the game."

That he was. Caminero — who finished the night 1-for-5 with two strikeouts — was ultimately overshadowed in the Game 4 box score by Aranda and Yandy Diaz, who combined for five hits and four RBI, including Diaz's ninth-inning, two-run homer that put the game out of reach. But Caminero's pair of particularly scorched batted balls can only portend good things as the Rays continue to push for a World Series berth.

"I have a lot of experience in this ballpark and know that it can be a little tricky on the cold nights," Cash said of Caminero's surprising non-homer. "Didn't look like there was a ton of wind, but that cool air can knock it down a little bit.

"But overall, just happy that Junior squared some balls up."

articles.title: Prediction markets are partnering with top athletes and sports teams. Why it’s taking the magic away for many fans
articles.summary: Partnerships between prediction markets and teams have for some, become emblematic of what fans see as unfettered greed permeating throughout sports.
articles.body: In college, JJ Allison was so successful at sports betting that even the friends of friends who functioned as low-level bookies stopped taking his money. That success translated to legal sports books as well when those debuted. Eventually they, like the bookies, didn’t want him betting with them either. His bets were limited to cents at a time. Prediction markets, however, don’t limit winners. That’s part of why Allison, now 25, prefers them and how he’s able to make a living as a professional prediction market trader. He’s steeped in these platforms, professionally invested, and not prone to conspiratorial concerns about insider trading or game fixing. And yet, when CNN Sports asked to speak with people who bet on sports but don’t like prediction markets partnering with sports leagues, teams or athletes themselves, Allison was among the dozens of fans who reached out. “While I’m obviously very invested in Prediction Markets, I think the permeation of ‘gambling’ into every fabric of society is incredibly detrimental,” he wrote in his initial email. Nowhere is that permeation more widespread than in sports. In the years since a Supreme Court ruling opened the door to legalized sports gambling in 2018, teams and leagues have embraced partnerships that have turned broadcasts, ballparks, arenas and, for a time, an entire regional sports network into billboards for sportsbooks like FanDuel and DraftKings. Eight years into this gambling frenzy, virtually every major sports league in America has one, if not multiple, partnerships with sports books. Most teams do as well. Leagues, like MLB and the NFL, have leveraged these partnerships to try to limit certain kinds of bets that are understood to be particularly vulnerable to manipulation. But the dangers and damages of even legalized sportsbooks are well documented. And their ubiquity, many fans say, feels increasingly oppressive. The result is that some sports enthusiasts who were initially excited about legal opportunities to bet on sports are now resentful of teams and leagues for “shoving it down everyone’s throat,” as 25-year-old Connor Lew from New York City told CNN Sports. These prediction market partnerships have, for some, become emblematic of what fans see as unfettered greed on the part of teams, players, leagues and platforms believed to be degrading their experience of sports writ large. “It’s another version of the fact that you have to have eight streaming platforms if you want to watch every game. They’re looking for every way to extract every last dollar from the fans, and that would be me,” said 54-year-old Rick Brody in Queens, NY. It is in this atmosphere of increasing backlash to sports gambling that nearly a quarter of MLB teams announced partnerships with prediction markets over the summer, following a league-level deal at the start of the season, and were met with a response that reflected not just fatigue, but betrayal. Asked if their particular concern was motivated by the prediction markets specifically or the broader encroachment of gambling into sports, fans differed. For some, the seemingly lax federal regulation and pending litigation around prediction markets raised alarm bells. For others, they lumped them in with sports books. The general consensus was that this latest wave of partnerships felt like a final straw, or a bridge too far. To them, it’s gambling creep – from the shadowy corners of offshore bookies to something mainstream superstar athletes are eager to promote. These fans don’t hate betting – plenty of them partake – but this is different. Many of those who spoke to CNN Sports said they feel like the thing that they love – the thing that connects them to their dad or their mom or their hometown or their friends – is making a mockery of that love. Many of them say these partnerships make the fan feel like a mark for helping the rich get richer. Allison worries everyday fans are being conditioned to see the diamond – or the court or the field – as slot machines and the human athletes as spinning symbols that sometimes align as dollar signs. “If you’re a family going to like the ballpark with your kids on a Saturday afternoon or something, I don’t think that gambling should really be a part of it,” Allison said. “I think that adding a money aspect just kind of incentivizes the wrong thing. “Like people may go and they say, ‘Oh, I’m rooting for the (New York) Yankees to win.’ And then in six years, most people at the Yankees game are there because they want to make money on the Yankees winning. And it’s not really about the Yankees winning or losing – it’s about them making money in the process.” CNN has a partnership with Kalshi and uses its data to cover major events, though CNN editorial employees are prohibited from trading on prediction platforms. The feeling that everyone’s making a buck off the fan When LeBron James announced a partnership with prediction market Polymarket on X – in a video featuring Eli Manning and Derek Jeter, among other celebrities – the replies were filled with accusations that he was “selling out.” “He’s just rubbing it in now huh,” one person posted in response. “It” here is something like financial security – wealth, and how it often seems that in order to have access to it, you must already possess it. The deal is reportedly worth $15 million a year, nearly four times what James is paid to play basketball for the Philadelphia 76ers. But also, to be more specific, it is how the adoration of sports fans made James a billionaire and gave the kid from Akron, Ohio, access to a space labeled “sports” but positioned – as shown on the elevator panel in the Polymarket ad – between “crypto” and the “economy.” What some people who spoke to CNN Sports saw in the ad was an exclusive club of sports celebs reveling in how good it is to be rich – laughing about being part of an inside joke where the punchline is the fans. “I hear rich people state all the time that money doesn’t buy happiness,” Brian Carroll, a 22-year-old professional gambler from Philadelphia, wrote in an email exchange after the partnership was announced, “then see people who already have more money than they could spend in 10 lifetimes willing to make the world worse to get more of it.” “I don’t feel like what I do is immoral. But I do think these things are bad,” he said of the prediction market partnerships when he spoke to CNN Sports before the ad was released. CNN Sports reached out to James’s agent for comment and did not receive a response. Backlash to MLB team partnerships Ahead of this season, Major League Baseball announced a league-level partnership with Polymarket. In July, the New York Mets became the first MLB team to strike an individual deal with a prediction market, partnering with the lesser-known peer-to-peer platform Novig. The announcement was flooded with critiques and the Mets’ post announcing the partnership on X was deleted and reposted multiple times. Soon after, the Yankees announced their own partnership with Polymarket. And then Kalshi announced it had partnered with five other teams, including the Los Angeles Dodgers. Some outlets speculated the muted rollout of Kalshi’s new partnerships was a response to the backlash the New York teams received, although the teams disputed that characterization to CNN Sports. (The Yankees declined to comment on their Polymarket partnership. The Dodgers and Boston Red Sox declined to comment on their Kalshi partnership. The Mets, Atlanta Braves and San Diego Padres did not reply to a request for comment.) “We’re pleased to welcome Kalshi to the Giants family,” said Steve Tseng, senior vice president of partnerships for the San Francisco Giants. “Creating unmatched experiences for our fans is a top priority, and we’re excited to work with Kalshi to deliver on that commitment.” In a statement, Novig said, in part, “The current online sportsbook model is predatory because sportsbooks make money when their customers lose, which creates inherently misaligned incentives. Our exchange model is different: we don’t profit from customer losses, winners are rewarded, and that makes for a fundamentally better product.” “We work with leagues and teams to give fans new ways to engage with the games they love, and with integrity built in from the start,” a Polymarket spokesperson said. Novig also pointed to its 21-and-older age requirement, which is unique among prediction markets. Kalshi did not comment on the fan frustrations specifically. As the law currently stands, prediction companies are treated like financial exchanges and are regulated by the federal government. But dozens of states argue that these companies offer gambling, and they’re fighting in courts across the country to apply their state gaming regulations. The companies are regulated on the federal level by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, or CFTC, which has historically focused on overseeing soybean futures and oil derivatives. And prediction platforms are required to police insider trading and report fraud on their sites, among other things. But in the words of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals, which ruled in August that states can regulate prediction market sites, “the CFTC is not a national gambling regulator.” There is no federal analogue to state laws that restrict deceptive marketing, promote responsible gaming and fund addiction programs. In contrast to other sports entering into partnerships with the prediction markets as they stand, the NFL recently came out in favor of increased regulation. The league, which accounts for the largest volume of trades on prediction markets, filed an amicus brief urging the Supreme Court to let states regulate prediction markets as they do sportsbooks. ‘It’s like when you find out Santa Claus ain’t real’ When CNN Sports put out a call on social media to talk to people who bet on sports but do not like their teams partnering with prediction markets, the callout received dozens of responses. The Kalshi CEO publicly criticized the line of inquiry, and that inspired another deluge of emails. Among the responses, accusations that that these partnerships are “predatory,” “slimy and scammy,” “disingenuous, if not completely hypocritical,” “disgusting,” “dirty,” “dangerous to young people,” and “all so f**king gross.” These are people who care enough about sports – a “sacred medium,” as John B. from Boston called it – to be concerned about these partnerships with prediction markets corrupting the space. They concede that some of this is probably just part of getting older and becoming more cynical about the financial motivations at the core of institutions preying on their emotional investment. And yet, these partnerships inspire a particular fury. “If you make it so overtly about the dollars, then it’s not the magical thing why people love it,” said Alexander Tsipis, a 30-year-old from Boston who was among more than a dozen people CNN Sports spoke to in depth about their objection to these partnerships. “It’s like when you find out Santa Claus ain’t real. Christmas starts to suck,” said Dustin Franklin, a 43-year-old attorney from Tennessee who now lives in West Virginia. “And that’s kind of what it is with gambling and sports.” “I personally think it’s sort of just like a late-stage capitalism thing,” says Miles Grossman, a 25-year-old aspiring sports broadcaster in the New York area. “As wealth gets more concentrated at the top, the masses feel like, ‘Well, I cannot possibly get rich, so at least I could possibly get a little money this way if I play my cards right.’” Grossman has been betting for more than half his life. His dad was a gambler – “what I’d like to call a very responsible sports bettor,” he says. After college, he worked at FanDuel for a stint. These days he gambles on both the legal sportsbooks and on Kalshi. But Grossman says betting and trading seems less cool – “loser s**t” as he puts it – now that they’re omnipresent and the dangers of gambling addiction are widely known. “The idea of getting rich off gambling is such a joke in 2026,” Grossman said. “Like there’s so many barriers to it.” At a time when cost of living is soaring and the job market is precarious, it’s not hard to fathom why more than a quarter of young people say sports gambling is part of their long-term financial plan. But Allison and Carroll are rare exceptions. Broadly speaking, fans don’t get rich from betting on sports – in fact, nearly one-third have gambling debt – and they don’t benefit from partnerships between betting platforms and their favorite teams. It doesn’t make the experience of watching or attending a game better or cheaper. It doesn’t make the on-field or on-court team more likely to win. “But what does come to fruition is some rich dude is getting richer at my f**king expense,” Franklin said. Undermining the public’s confidence? Nobody CNN Sports spoke to speculated that the prediction market partnerships were currently tied to any nefarious schemes within sports. But most mentioned that the increased integration between gambling and sports would inevitably erode public confidence in the product over time. “Not that I’m saying any one individual I would suspect of doing something fraudulent, but it’s just so obviously present as a potential that it’s scary,” said Bobby Fallarino, a 32-year-old teacher from Queens, New York. It’s an optics issue as much as anything else. When scandals are revealed, teams and leagues with close ties to gambling companies are accused of hypocrisy. (It’s worth noting, the CFTC has proposed limiting markets that are especially vulnerable to individual actors.) When the officiating feels unfair or there’s a late-game swing in fortunes that meaningfully alters the outcome, “You start asking, ‘Is the fix in?’ or whatever. Instead of just being like, ‘Oh, that’s crazy,’” said Ben Gibson, a 40-year-old from North Carolina. A Polymarket spokesperson responded to concerns about insider trading by saying, “Insider trading is banned on our platforms, and athletes, coaches, officials and anyone else who can influence an outcome can’t trade. We enforce those rules with advanced, real-time surveillance. We restrict accounts, refer cases to authorities, and strict monitoring has helped lead to federal insider-trading charges. Our league partnerships also let leagues see trading around their games and flag concerns directly.” And Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said, “Insider trading happens in all financial markets, from stock markets to prediction markets. Prediction markets distill trading into a single question — narrowing the range of information material to a traded event contract. We may see different types of insiders trying to break the rules, but it also may be simpler to prove insider trading in some of these cases because the material info is narrower and easier to identify. On Kalshi, and under federal law, insider trading is banned. We surveil, investigate, and punish it.” But that doesn’t mean the perception isn’t out there. “People are a lot more likely, I think, to lean into the implication now,” Gibson said of the conspiracy thinking that can follow a controversial call that leads to losing money. “I think the leagues can only blame themselves because this is who they’re partnering with.” And even the respondents who are skeptical of anything actually affecting the integrity of the games, are concerned about the possibility – known to exist beyond sports – of insider trading on the prediction markets. “From layman’s perspective, it just seems like it’s a platform that lends itself so much more to the insider trading,” said Jorge Adames-Reyes, a 25-year-old Harvard Law student, who pointed to what he called a “refreshingly bipartisan effort” to litigate prediction markets as evidence that these platforms have not been sufficiently vetted. At least some of the team partnerships are only through the end of this baseball season. MLB’s league-wide deal reportedly includes exit-clauses in case the legality of prediction markets change. “But in the meantime, (the message seems to be), ‘We’re happy for you to spend your money with us and watch a Mets broadcast and be exposed to Novig commercials,’” Adames-Reyes added. “I think that’s the part that ideologically just makes me feel really uneasy.” Why it matters so much to fans Fans are eager to talk about these prediction market partnerships because they want the people in positions of power to understand that they’re not stupid, even if they find themselves as pawns in enriching people on either side of the deals. No one said they would stop watching their favorite team or betting as the result of these partnerships, but fans still express frustration. “They really are just laughing in your face because Kalshi knows (Milwaukee) Bucks fans aren’t going to stop rooting for Giannis,” Franklin said (referring to Giannis Antetokounmpo’s team at the time of the deal) – and that extends to fans of any team or player with a prediction market partnership. Even the winners understand that gambling on sports comes at a cost. “With betting, it’s very much an anti-fandom,” Carroll, the professional gambler from Philadelphia, said. “Like, it makes it less fun to watch sports.” And sometimes, you have to lose to retain any fun at all. Allison, the professional prediction market trader living in Miami, watched the Super Bowl in Las Vegas this year – epicenter of sports gambling – surrounded by neutral fans. But as a kid, he watched New England Patriots games at home in Massachusetts. The rational part of him that knows how to empirically assess a smart bet knew he should put his money on the Seattle Seahawks to win. “But I kind of felt this moment of betrayal,” he said reflecting on that experience. “Here I am at 25 years old now, betting against the team that I grew up rooting for because I think it’ll make me money. And I felt almost disgusted with that idea.” So, he didn’t. Allison put a little bit of money on the Patriots. They lost, and so did he. Even though he broadly benefits from the system that allows wagering on sports, in this instance he sacrificed some amount of money to prioritize the purity of the fan experience. Fans just want their favorite players, teams and leagues to do the same.

articles.title: Yankees Should Trade for Jacob Young Amid World Series Title Drought, MLB Rumors
articles.summary: The New York Yankees previously expressed interest in Washington Nationals center fielder Jacob Young, Joel Sherman of the New York Post reported (h/t MLBTradeRumors.com).
articles.body:
The New York Yankees previously expressed interest in Washington Nationals center fielder Jacob Young, Joel Sherman of the New York Post reported (h/t MLBTradeRumors.com ).

While the team did not execute a trade for the 27-year-old last January, it is a potential deal the organization must revisit as it continues its hunt for its first World Series title since 2009.

Young is not going to electrify anyone at the plate. He is not the home run threat that Aaron Judge is, hitting just 10 home runs in 2026. Instead, he impacts the game in two other areas, both benefiting the Bronx Bombers.

Ranking Tarik Skubal's Top Landing Spots 🛬

In four Major League seasons, Young has stolen 79 bases. That is a significant boost to the offense and helps to put the team in scoring position, even when the bats aren't on fire. It is, inarguably, his greatest offensive asset.

He hit .252 this past season, with 10 home runs, and a 2.3 WAR.

He is also a defender in the outfield, landing in the top 10 in defensive WAR in two of the last three seasons. He currently sits at +49 Outs Above Average, second only to likely NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs.

He is also a two-time Gold Glove finalist, further validating his superb play in center field.

There is an argument to be made that the Yankees do not need another outfielder, with Aaron Judge, Spencer Jones, and Cody Bellinger rounding out that portion of the lineup.

Judge has spent the last few seasons fending off injuries or missing big chunks of time due to them, though, and having someone who can take the load off of him and reduce his need to place in the outfield could be beneficial to the team and player.

It would open up the possibility to shuffle around the outfield and even give Jones the opportunity to grow into the role, without placing pressure for him to excel as a defender before he is ready.

With Jasson Dominguez not making the impact some expected, or even having the consistent opportunity to do so, and Heliot Ramos a potential option, the Yankees have the pieces to make a trade.

Considering Young is eligible for arbitration in 2027, has club control through 2029, and is the most affordable of the three young centerpieces of the Nationals' lineup, it is a deal the Yankees must consider making.

After all, the organization has built its reputation on championships, and it is nearing two decades without one. Acquiring a player who can prevent runs and set others up with his work on the basepaths certainly will not hurt their chances of ending that drought, nor will what is almost certain to be a modest price tag.

articles.title: Former MLB star Jimmy Rollins was not hacked, he is the co-founder of a women's underwear brand
articles.summary: Jimmy Rollins' Instagram posts left fans wondering if he'd been hacked, but the Phillies great revealed his co-founded underwear brand venture.
articles.body: A few days ago, there was some speculation online that Jimmy Rollins was either hacked or "out here getting his freak on" after a couple Instagram posts seemingly out of left field. Neither was the case. The posts were part of a business venture the 47-year-old retired MLB star has gotten himself into. In between his analyst role for TNT Sports and sinking hole-in-ones for luxury boats, the 2007 NL MVP has "redesigned the panty." A noble endeavor that has apparently paid off. The first of the posts that caught his followers off-guard included screenshots of text messages about how amazing The Pretty Kitty Klub is. That's the underwear brand he co-founded. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Jimmy wrote, "Texts like this lets us know that @theprettykittyklub is doing its job and saving sex lives one marriage at a time 😂." Understandably, this post following one that declared "postseason defense matters!" had people wondering if he had been hacked. Rarely do you see that much range from post to post on Instagram. But it was real. Jimmy Rollins hadn't been hacked. He had indeed been out there saving marriages by rethinking the design of women's underwear. SYDNEY SWEENEY AND LIVVY DUNNE FORM ALLIANCE AS LINGERIE WAR WITH VICTORIA'S SECRET OFFICIALLY HEATS UP The second post had models in the product and a message about the upcoming holiday season. It was a doubling down that had more questions filling up the comment section. "Okay everyone keeps texting and asking but I can’t name names, what I can do is give a glimpse of @theprettykittyklub," the Phillies great wrote. "Fellas remember it’s holiday season, get yourself a gift…for her 😜 and to all the Ladies comfy and sexy does exist, treat yourself and you can thank me later. (All the models and scenes are real, AI helped me edit 🤷🏾‍♂️)" While there were a lot of folks wondering what was going on, and where this had all come from? He did have fans who had grown up with him willing to go along with it. Without any answers. "I had a lifesize poster of you on my wall as a kid," one fan wrote. "I guess this is what I’m getting my girl for xmas now😂" Another added, "Is my 🐐 ok? I’m a guy but if World Series champion and Phillies legend j-roll says so I’ll buy some." OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD The company confirmed that up until last week Jimmy had been taking a more private role with the company. "Mr. Rollins is a co-founder of Pretty Kitty Klub," they told NY Post in a statement. "Jimmy has taken a more private role, focused on the company’s long-term vision, strategic growth, and business development. That’s why he isn’t currently featured on the website." Dream big and have more than one. Life doesn’t end once you hang up the cleats. There is more work to be done and women's underwear to redesign.

articles.title: Dodgers 2026 report card: Tarik Skubal trade not enough to save banged-up pitching staff
articles.summary: The last two years, the Dodgers’ pitching staff carried them to World Series titles –– with the bullpen doing the heavy lifting in 2024, and the rotation pit...
articles.body:
The last two years, the Dodgers' pitching staff carried them to World Series titles –– with the bullpen doing the heavy lifting in 2024, and the rotation pitching at a superhuman level in 2025.

This season, the group couldn't replicate that success, enduring adversity during an injury-plagued regular season and then failure against a relentless Brewers offense in the team's National League Championship Series elimination .

Still, the Dodgers boasted a talented staff, finishing with the fourth-lowest team ERA in the majors this year.

In Part 2 of the California Post's end-of-season report card for the Dodgers' 2026 season , here's a look at how each key arm performed, and where they stand entering 2027:

It's worth remembering: Yamamoto entered 2026 coming off a career-high 30 regular-season starts in 2025, another 37 innings in his heroic postseason run, and an appearance this spring in the World Baseball Classic. You'd have been forgiven for thinking his right arm was about to fall off.

Instead, the reigning World Series MVP was even more productive in 2026, throwing more innings (185), collecting more wins (14-9 record) and lowering his WHIP (0.87) while posting a nearly-identical 2.53 ERA (fifth-lowest in the majors). The only disappointment: He didn't replicate last year's historic October, suffering the Dodgers' shortest playoff start during a pivotal NLCS Game 2 loss . Still, he's on the (very) short list for best pitchers in the game right now.

Another member of that short list, Skubal just about lived up to the billing following his blockbuster trade deadline deal, going 5-2 with a 2.61 ERA in his 10 regular-season starts for the Dodgers. He also had the best postseason of anyone in their rotation, giving up three runs over 11 innings in two starts.

Still, he took the defeat in his NLCS outing. And in the end, the team's aggressive acquisition of the two-time Cy Young Award winner didn't work out as intended, failing to help the team complete a World Series three-peat. The question now: Will the Dodgers be as aggressive in trying to re-sign him as a free agent ?

This was not the season Blake Snell was envisioning . He was limited to just nine starts by shoulder and elbow injuries. And though he did post a minuscule 1.90 ERA in the regular season, he suffered two disastrous playoff starts, failing to complete four innings against the Braves in one and giving up back-to-back seventh-inning home runs against the Brewers in the other. He showed he still has some of the best stuff in the sport when right. But after another abbreviated regular season, the Dodgers needed more from him in October.

Glasnow's season was similar to Snell's. He made just 13 regular-season starts because of back problems, going 5-2 with a 3.53 ERA. His performance also regressed in the playoffs, when he blew a four-run lead with the team facing elimination in Game 4 of the NLCS. The last couple years, the Dodgers have gotten away with limited workloads from both pitchers. But next year, they will be expecting more from each of them, in the regular season and the playoffs.

Wrobleski was having an A+ season through mid-July, going from bullpen swingman to breakout rotation star with an 11-2 record and 2.62 ERA through his first 17 outings. However, the All-Star selection finished on a sour note, getting shifted to the bullpen after a serious bout with home run struggles down the stretch. He showed he can be a quality big-league starter. Now he needs to prove he can do it over the course of a full year.

What started as a rollercoaster campaign for the second-year Japanese phenom finished with signs of tangible progress . In his first 15 starts, Sasaki had a 5.40 ERA and 1.47 WHIP. In his next seven starts after that, he had a 2.63 ERA and 1.21 WHIP, finding success with a reworked arsenal and improved command. A blister sidetracked that late-season surge, and prompted a shift back to the bullpen for the playoffs. But entering 2027, the Dodgers will be hoping he can take another step. Finally, they have real reason to believe he can.

This was largely a lost season for Sheehan, whose first full campaign back from Tommy John surgery did not go according to plan. He was 5-8 with a 4.57 ERA in 23 outings. He battled inconsistent velocity and mechanics. He was sent back to triple-A for much of the final two months. He did seem to find something late in the year, giving up only one run over 17 innings in three September outings. But he has a big offseason ahead if he wants to re-cement himself as a long-term fixture in the Dodgers' rotation.

For most of the year, nothing went right for the $69 million offseason signing . He battled elbow and neck injuries. He posted a career-worst 8.68 ERA in the regular season. He was nearly left off the team's postseason roster. Despite all that, he did finish the year as the Dodgers' expected, rediscovering his typically dominant form just in time to return to the closer's role in October. But that was the only silver lining to take from an otherwise dismal debut Dodgers season.

The Edwin Díaz of 2025, Scott was significantly better in the second year of his $72 million deal. He had 25 saves and a 2.69 ERA, one of only 11 pitchers to do so this year. His 82 strikeouts were most of the Dodgers' bullpen. However, he also gave up a pair of postseason home runs, including a go-ahead shot in their NLCS Game 4 elimination. In other words, while he was better in 2026, he still hasn't lived up to his big contract.

Henriquez was a bit of a revelation in his first full MLB season, posting a 2.85 ERA in 61 outings while wowing with his 100.7 mph average fastball (second-hardest in the majors behind only Mason Miller). His postseason was forgettable. But, moving forward, he should be a key arm in the Dodgers' bullpen long-term.

The pending free agent had another solid season, posting a sub-3.02 ERA (2.64) for the fifth time in six years with the Dodgers. Before the playoffs, he expressed his hope of being back in Los Angeles next year. But, he should have plenty of other suitors on the open market this winter.

It took time for Phillips to knock the rust off following his return from Tommy John. But by the end of the year, his fastball was back in the upper-90s (even hitting 100 at one point). After re-signing with the Dodgers last year, he hits free agency again this offseason.

When healthy, Stewart was effective. But he continued his career-long battle with injuries, making only 28 appearances. He enters his final season of team control in 2027.

Treinen never quite looked right this year, while spending extended time on the injured list for a second-straight season. A season-ending shoulder injury also put the 38-year-old's future in question. At the very least, it's possible the soon-to-be free agent might have thrown his last pitch for the Dodgers after a decorated seven-year tenure.

Last year's World Series hero was good in the first half, but ultimately finished the year with a 3.67 ERA and elbow troubles. He should get another chance to prove himself as a high-leverage big-league reliever in 2027.

It was a decent season overall for Dreyer (3.20 ERA). But a September slump cost him a spot on the Dodgers' postseason roster. He'll be trying to increase his role in 2027.

Lauer served his purpose this year, giving the Dodgers reliable starts amid a midseason injury crisis to the rest of their rotation. As a free agent, however, he will likely have to look elsewhere for starting opportunities in 2027.

Once a highly-touted prospect who had dealt with injuries in recent years, Hurt made 44 appearances this year but had an up-and-down campaign that finished with a 4.14 ERA. He'll be one of many fringe arms trying to earn a big-league job in spring training next year.

articles.title: Deseret News archives: This is why they call Reggie Jackson ‘Mr. October’
articles.summary: On this day in 1977, Jackson cracked three home runs to lead the Yankees past the Dodgers in the deciding World Series game.
articles.body:
Editor's note: This story was originally published on Oct 18, 2024.

A look back at local, national and world events through Deseret News archives.

On Oct. 18, 1977, Reggie Jackson hit three home runs in Game 6 of the World Series to lead the New York Yankees to an 8-4 win and a 4-2 Series victory over the Los Angeles Dodgers; his success in the Fall Classic earned him the nickname "Mr. October."

Jackson is a true baseball character, a showman who happened to also be a great ballplayer. That he spent his career squabbling with his own team (such as Charlie Finley, Billy Martin, George Steinbrenner) only added to the persona.

And after the 1977 World Series, he became Mr. October.

For the record, Jackson, a hard-hitting outfielder/first baseman, played 1,045 games with the Oakland Athletics, 653 with the Yankees. He was the key position-player when the A's won five consecutive divisional and three World Series titles in the early and mid-1970s. He also played for the Baltimore Orioles and California Angels.

He was inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1993.

Jackson cracked 563 homes, 14th best in MLB history, and won just about every award during his long career. He also holds the most career strikeouts record. Most notably, he was a part of a winning team for 19 of the 21 years he played. Outspoken, he did battle teammates, his managers and owners, through his career.

The '77 World Series was a great battle between the longtime rivals, who may meet again in a week for another World Series showdown.

The Yankees won the opener in 12 innings, but the Dodgers evened the series up in Game 2. The Yankees won the next two games, but the Dodgers stayed alive with an easy win in Game 5.

Back in New York for Game 6, the Dodgers owned a 3-2 lead after three innings, but then Jackson got to work. First came a two-run homer off Burt Hooton in the fourth. Just an inning later, Jackson again blasted a two-run shot, this one off Elias Sosa. And he finished off his power display with a solo clout off Charlie Hough in the eighth, propelling the Bronx Bombers to an 8-4 Series-clinching victory.

Thus was born Mr. October. Newspapers loved Reggie Jackson and his career exploits.

The next year, at the Yankees' home opener, the Reggie Bar was handed out to more than 50,000 fans entering Yankee Stadium.

Jackson homered, of course, and fans showered the field with Reggie Bars.

articles.title: Major League Baseball's best team can't stop pretending to be the underdogs heading into World Series
articles.summary: Milwaukee Brewers manager Pat Murphy once again played the ridiculous underdog card after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers, but will it continue against Cleveland or Tampa?
articles.body: The American League Championship Series is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday evening's game five. After the Tampa Bay Rays offense scuffled against the Cleveland Guardians' pitching staff, they finally broke through in game four thanks to Yandy Diaz, Jonathan Aranda and Richie Palacios. Not exactly the most famous names in Major League Baseball, sure, but an example of the Rays' depth and ability to create tough matchups for opposing pitchers up and down the lineup. Game five will pair two of the top ten pitchers in baseball in 2026, by FanGraphs WAR, Drew Rasmussen and Parker Messick. Again, not the most well-known names, sure, but based on performance, those two pitchers outperformed highly paid, big-name starters like Zack Wheeler, Framber Valdez, Kevin Gausman or Max Fried. Given the inherent volatility and randomness of postseason baseball, trying to draw permanent or predictive conclusions from small sample size outcomes is ultimately pointless. But there is one clear pattern that's been obvious for years and become even more apparent in 2026: there are no underdogs in the playoffs. So why is the best team in baseball still acting like one? WANT TO KNOW HOW TO WIN IN OCTOBER? THE 2026 MILWAUKEE BREWERS ARE PROVIDING THE BLUEPRINT On the other side of the tournament bracket, the Milwaukee Brewers swept the very expensive Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS. The Brewers bullpen, behind Aaron Ashby, DL Hall, JoJo Romero, Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill, among others, was virtually unhittable. Well, not necessarily unhittable, but impossible to score runs against. Those pitchers allowed just two runs in 15.2 innings of relief in the NLCS, both from Uribe. In 13 innings from Ashby, Hall, Romero and Megill, not one runner who reached base scored. Not one. League-wide, the average left on base rate is roughly 75%. For Milwaukee's bullpen, outside one outing from Uribe, it was 100%. Offensively, it was more of the same. League average for batting average on balls put in play is around .300. Here's the Milwaukee BABIP from the LCS: BREWERS OFFICIALLY END DODGERS DYNASTY WITH RIDICULOUS 6-4 COMEBACK IN GAME FOUR TO COMPLETE NLCS SWEEP Hilariously, Garrett Mitchell had a .000 BABIP because his only two hits were series-changing home runs off left-handed starting pitchers, despite having just two homers off lefties in his entire career. Milwaukee's starting pitchers, too, allowed just three earned runs, despite woeful strikeout-walk percentages of 0%, 10% and 10.5%. Much of that comes down to, again, the randomness that's part of small sample sizes. Weird things happen in three or four games throughout the regular season all the time, without anyone noticing or caring. But with the spotlight on, outcomes become part of some mystical, usually made-up approach or perceived grittiness. The Brewers this postseason have been credited by baseball analysts for their supposed plan to put the ball in play. Make contact, see what happens, instead of just selling out for home runs and striking out instead. What actually happened? Milwaukee outhomered the Dodgers 7-1 and had the highest "three true outcomes," or strikeouts-walks-home runs, rate of any team in postseason history. Whatever the Brewers' plan actually was, the reality is that their approach was exactly the one that analysts, former players paid handsomely to give their "expert" opinions and fans claim doesn't work in October. Clearly, it works. Regardless, while the series might have had fluky components, between Milwaukee's fortunate luck on balls in play, runners in scoring position performance and pitching outcomes, the ultimate series result was anything but. The Brewers were once again the best team in baseball in 2026, just as they were in 2025. They had the best run differential in baseball, at +214. For reference, they were more than 170 runs better, over one run per game, better, than the very expensive San Diego Padres team they beat in the division series round. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE They've won more games than anyone in baseball since the start of the 2025 season. They were the best team in the league when it comes to outscoring their opponents over the course of the 2026 season. Before the NLCS, 13 of 15 ESPN writers picked the Brewers to beat the Dodgers. So why do they keep acting like nobody believes in them? In 2025, Brewers manager Pat Murphy played the underdog card before that year's NLCS, acting as though his opponent had not heard of the team they were facing. "I'm sure that most Dodger players can't name eight guys on our roster," Murphy told reporters. "No offense to them, they shouldn't have to know the names, but these are some guys that hopefully they know their names by the time it's over. You never know." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! As insufferable and absurd as that was, Murphy continued in the middle of the 2026 season, acting like his team's biggest division rival had also not heard of his players who were currently in first place. "We know how these series go, you know, you erase it and just keep going," Murphy said about the Chicago Cubs. "It's not necessarily a game where they're ever going to be intimidated by guys, they don't even know most of our guys' names, so they're never going to be intimidated by us, but we're not looking for that." Yes, of course, nobody knows the players on the team in first place in the division. You'd think that after winning 103 games, performing as the consensus best team in baseball, and sweeping the NLCS, Murphy would drop his shtick, but he couldn't even wait a few minutes before trotting it out yet again in the game four postgame celebrations. "They got a bunch of hall of famers," Murphy said about the Dodgers. "We got a bunch of gamers. And the gamers won this week." Ah. Sure. Of course the Dodgers have an exceptional amount of talent, including Hall of Famers like Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman and Mookie Betts. The Brewers have an exceptional amount of talent too, and Murphy's routine of pretending like his team is a bunch of humble farmers who were playing stickball out back a few days ago is absurd and offensive. Though apparently diminishing his own roster is part of the team's motivational playbook. Jacob Misiorowski is 24-years-old, and a near-lock to win the NL Cy Young Award. He's so overwhelming that he was added to the 2025 NL All-Star team after just a handful of appearances in the big leagues. Obviously, Misiorowski is very early in his career, but who's to say he won't be a Hall of Famer later on? He's certainly on track after a year and a half. Misiorowski's salary is artificially limited by MLB's rules that punish young players, but were he available on the open market, he'd be making $50-60 million this season. Jackson Chourio is only 22 and just set the MLB record for most home runs in a postseason career before turning 23. If that's not the start of a potential Hall of Fame career, what is? Chourio signed an $82 million contract with Milwaukee already that would have been significantly higher were it not buying out years of cheap team control. He's a three-time Silver Slugger Award winner, three-time All-Star and two-time batting champion. If he doesn't make the Hall of Fame, he'll certainly come up just short. Brice Turang was a first round draft pick who won a Platinum Glove for his defense in 2024. Garrett Mitchell is another former first round pick out of UCLA. Total nobody. Logan Henderson was a top-100 prospect entering the season. Jake Bauers has been awful for most of his career, but graduated in 2018 as a top-50 prospect. William Contreras has been so good in his five years as a starter that he already ranks No. 96 in career WAR among all catchers in baseball history. Should he keep up this pace for 10 more seasons, he'd amass 60 career WAR, putting him eighth all time at his position, ahead of surefire Hall of Famers like Buster Posey and Yadier Molina. Like most playoff series, the only actual secret is having a pretty good team and hoping you get hot, and/or lucky, at the right time. That's what happened here. Pretending like they're hapless underdogs when, again, they are the best team in baseball, is ridiculous. Yes, the Dodgers have higher paid players. The Tampa Bay Rays are one win away from reaching the World Series.

The Rays downed the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 of the American League Championship Series on Sunday behind a strong performance from starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen.

Brewers reach World Series for 1st time since 1982

It was all Tampa Bay through the majority of the game.

The Rays got on the board in the top of the first inning when Jonny DeLuca drew a bases-loaded walk against Parker Messick. Tampa Bay added another in the top of the second when Jonathan Aranda singled to left field to drive in a run.

Liam Hicks made it a 3-0 game in the top of the third, and the Rays nearly added another run in the fourth inning, but a tremendous throw from Steven Kwan prevented further damage.

After five shutout innings from Drew Rasmussen, Cleveland finally got on the board on a fielder's choice in the bottom of the sixth to cut the deficit to two runs.

In the top of the ninth, the Rays had the chance to do more damage, but Kwan came through with another outstanding defensive play to prevent extra bases.

The Guardians had the heart of the order up in the bottom of the ninth as they tried to either win it or force extra innings, and Chase DeLauter drew a walk to get the tying run to the plate.

Jo Adell then grounded it to the shortstop, Taylor Walls, who got DeLauter at second but couldn't get Adell out at first. Nathaniel Lowe's foul ball was caught for the second out, and Travis Bazzana grounded out to end the game.

The Rays, who are seeking their first World Series appearance since 2020, will have the chance to close out the series at home on Monday.

articles.title: Rasmussen shines as Rays beat Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 to take a 3-2 ALCS lead
articles.summary: Drew Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win, Tampa Bay’s offense kept up constant pressure, and the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 on Sunday night to take a 3-2 lead in the AL Championship Series.
articles.body: Drew Rasmussen allowed one run over seven innings for his second postseason win, Tampa Bay’s offense kept up constant pressure, and the Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 on Sunday night to take a 3-2 lead in the AL Championship Series. The Rays will try to capture their third AL pennant and first since 2020 on Monday at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida. Since the ALCS expanded to seven games in 1985, road teams winning Game 5 for a 3-2 lead have won the series four of five times. Game 7, if needed, would be Tuesday, and the World Series starts Friday at NL champion Milwaukee. Cleveland has not won an ALCS when trailing 3-2. Tampa Bay scored single runs in each of the first three innings, the first two off Parker Messick and the third against Tim Herrin. Rasmussen shut down the Guardians’ offense after allowing two runs over six innings in the opener. After Chase DeLauter’s two-out single in the first, the 31-year-old right-hander retired nine straight batters and allowed only one other baserunner through the sixth. Rasmussen gave up four hits, walked one and struck out six. He is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA in three postseason starts, striking out 23 and walking three. Cam Booser and Tyler Wells worked the eighth, with Wells striking out José Ramírez to strand a runner. Bryan Baker came in for the ninth and converted his 35th straight save chance, his fifth of this postseason. Jo Adell was on second base when Travis Bazzana hit a game-ending groundout. Steven Kwan had two of Cleveland’s five hits and made two fine defensive plays: He threw out Taylor Walls trying to score from second base on Jonathan Aranda’s fourth-inning single to left and made a leaping catch at the center-field wall on Victor Mesa Jr.’s eighth-inning drive, saving a run. Tampa Bay’s leadoff hitter reached base in the first four innings — scoring in the first three frames — and six times overall. Rays leadoff batters have reached in 10 of 14 innings dating to Saturday. Yandy Díaz had three hits while Aranda and Liam Hicks both had two hits and drove in a run. Díaz scored on a bases-loaded walk by Messick to Jonny DeLuca in the first inning. Díaz led off with a line-drive double over center fielder Petey Halpin that rolled to the wall. Aranda’s single drove in Ben Williamson for a 2-0 lead in the second, and Hicks looped a curveball from Herrin to center to score Chandler Simpson in the third. Cleveland finally threatened in the seventh when Kwan and Ramírez singled to put runners at the corners and DeLauter grounded an RBI single between first and second. Messick had the shortest outing of his big-league career and didn’t make it past the third inning for the second time in four postseason starts. The 25-year-old left-hander allowed two runs, five hits and three walks over two innings, throwing just 34 of 57 pitches for strikes.

articles.title: Drew Rasmussen wins the pitchers' duel that wasn't as Rays move within a win of World Series berth
articles.summary: The Rays beat the Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 to take a 3-2 lead in the ALCS.
articles.body:
CLEVELAND — A pivotal ALCS Game 5 that looked on paper like a premium pitchers' duel dissolved into something much different on Sunday, as the Tampa Bay Rays took down the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 at Progressive Field to move within one win of a World Series berth. While the final score suggests a closely contested ballgame, the tale of the two starting pitchers tells otherwise.

When the AL Cy Young Award is announced next month, it's a safe bet that New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler will take home the honor. Toronto's Dylan Cease appears to be the likeliest runner-up. Beyond that, both Rays right-hander Drew Rasmussen and Guardians rookie lefty Parker Messick have a strong case to be the third finalist, based on their fantastic regular seasons. Rasmussen ranked third in fWAR (5.0) and fourth in ERA (2.67) behind Schlittler and Cease; Messick ranked fourth in fWAR (4.9) and third in ERA (2.56).

These were the starting pitchers for Game 5 on Sunday. Rasmussen had tossed six innings of two-run ball in Game 1 — but in a Rays loss. Messick covered five innings and allowed three runs in Game 2 — but in a Guardians loss. With the series tied at two games apiece, Sunday's contest gave each frontline arm the tantalizing chance to push his club closer to the American League pennant.

For neutral observers hoping for maximum October drama, the blueprint for a best-case clash could be found in July, when Rasmussen and Messick traded blows in a 1-0 Rays victory at Tropicana Field . In that one, Messick allowed the lone run across 7 ⅔ innings while Rasmussen yielded just one hit across seven shutout frames. If a similar game were on tap Sunday — this time with supremely elevated stakes — that would mean a timely hit or two would be required to seize a narrow victory. But such visions of a repeat nailbiter enforced by these elite starters were quashed in a hurry.

On Sunday, the Rays exhausted Messick from the get-go, quickly eliminating any chance of a classic postseason pitching showdown. While the standout rookie southpaw's velocity has sustained this season even as his workload has extended well beyond his previous career highs, his command has notably faltered in recent weeks. Messick struck out Junior Caminero twice with changeups in the first two innings, but that's about all that went well for the lefty. Although he allowed only one extra-base hit (Yandy Díaz's double to lead off the game) and two runs, the pesky Rays lineup forced him to throw 31 pitches in the first inning and 26 in the second, prompting Cleveland manager Stephen Vogt to turn to his bullpen far earlier than planned

A Chandler Simpson leadoff double followed by a Liam Hicks RBI single made it 3-0 Tampa Bay in the third inning against Tim Herrin, the second of six Cleveland hurlers who took the mound in a losing effort Sunday. That was a comfortable enough cushion for Rasmussen, who held up his end of the bargain for those hoping to see some top-notch starting pitching.

Rasmussen's excellence was on full display in his first start of October, when he carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning against the Yankees in the ALDS, but he was not as sharp six days ago in the series opener against Cleveland . The turning point in Game 1 came when Rays manager Kevin Cash entrusted Rasmussen, at 90 pitches, to tackle the bottom of Cleveland's order in the seventh inning with a 2-1 lead. Then Guardians catcher Patrick Bailey ambushed a first-pitch cutter and launched it for a game-tying solo shot that spoiled Rasmussen's solid effort. From there, the Guardians piled on against the Rays' bullpen en route to a 7-3 victory.

A similar scenario arrived late in Rasmussen's Game 5 outing. The right-hander had cruised through five scoreless innings but he surrendered a run in the sixth to make it 3-1. The bottom portion of Cleveland's order was scheduled to hit in the seventh, and Rasmussen had thrown 83 pitches. Cash stuck with his ace again, and this time, he was rewarded.

After Nathaniel Lowe led off with a single, Rasmussen won a seven-pitch battle with Guardians rookie Travis Bazzana that ended in a harmless popout. Then Rasmussen exacted revenge on Bailey for his Game 1 blast, inducing an inning-ending double play to punctuate his outing and complete seven innings of one-run ball. It was a vintage Rasmussen performance, with his three fastballs (four-seam, sinker, cutter) keeping hitters off-balance and a heavier dose of changeups coaxing whiffs and weak contact all night long.

"It is really fun because there's so much more setting guys up," Hicks said of working with Rasmussen behind the plate. "You're thinking along a lot more — it's not just power, where you're just trying to beat the guy with the stuff. I think just with how good our defense is, you really have the trust [that] we don't always need a strikeout."

Tampa Bay's terrific Game 5 pitching did not end with Rasmussen. Lefty Cam Booser recorded the first two outs of the eighth before Steven Kwan lined a single to center to bring up José Ramírez as the tying run. Cash called on Tyler Wells to take on Ramírez, and Wells delivered, getting Ramirez to swing through a cutter up and away for an inning-ending strikeout. He pumped his fists and bounced off the mound, knowing he'd completed the bridge to closer Bryan Baker.

"It's probably the biggest at-bat of my career so far," Wells reflected afterward. "You don't sit there and take that stuff for granted. You go out there, and you want to compete, and you want to come up big, but you can't force it. You got to go out there and execute pitches. And I was just grateful to be in the game at that time and just try to soak it all in and enjoy it."

Baker's save opportunity started with a leadoff walk to DeLauter, but the All-Star right-hander retired the next three batters to finalize the 3-1 victory and push Tampa Bay just one win away from the World Series. Cleveland finished the game without an extra-base hit for the first time this postseason.

The ALCS now shifts back to Tropicana Field for Game 6 on Monday, an unusually quick turnaround after Friday's rainout eliminated the scheduled travel day on Sunday . The Rays will give the ball to Freddy Peralta, who shined in Game 2 and made a successful (albeit brief) relief appearance in Game 4 .

Cleveland is still sorting out its pitching plans, with Vogt saying postgame Sunday that Gavin Williams is not an option to start Monday on short rest after he threw 70 pitches across five innings on Thursday (and his velocity notably dipped in his final inning). The Guardians will need to find a way to force Game 7 if they are to give Williams another chance to add to his fantastic October to date.

Díaz, the only player on the Rays' ALCS roster who appeared in the Fall Classic with Tampa Bay in 2020, sat on the podium Sunday after a three-hit performance and spoke of what lies ahead in no uncertain terms .

"It's a great opportunity," Díaz said through interpreter Kevin Vera of being one win away from the World Series. "All of us are thinking of it.

"But it all ends tomorrow. We're going to win tomorrow."
